description: Functions that call themselves — and the two rules that keep them safe.

screens.body: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller piece of the same problem. Like standing between two mirrors: the reflection contains a smaller reflection, which contains a smaller one… Each call handles one layer and trusts the deeper calls to handle the rest.
screens.heading: What is recursion?
screens.keyPoint: A function calling itself on a smaller problem.

screens.body: Every recursive function needs a base case — the simple input where it stops calling itself and just returns an answer. factorial(0) = 1. That's the bottom of the mirrors. Without a base case, the calls never stop: infinite recursion, then a stack overflow crash.

options: Where the recursion stops and returns
The first line of the function
check.question: The base case is…

screens.heading: Rule 1: the base case
screens.keyPoint: No base case = infinite calls = crash.

screens.body: Each recursive call must work on a SMALLER input than the one it got — n-1, a shorter string, half the array. If the input doesn't shrink, you never reach the base case. Two rules, that's all: stop somewhere, and shrink every step.
screens.heading: Rule 2: smaller every time

screens.body: factorial(3) calls factorial(2), which calls factorial(1), which calls factorial(0) → returns 1. Then the answers bubble back up: 1×1=1, 2×1=2, 3×2=6. The calls pile up going down, then resolve coming back up.

check.question: factorial(3) makes how many calls total?

screens.heading: Trace it: factorial(3)
screens.keyPoint: Calls pile up, answers bubble back.

screens.body: Every time a function calls itself, the current call waits on the call stack while the new one runs. Deep recursion = tall stack. That's why 'stack overflow' is literally the stack running out of room — too many waiting calls.

options: Calls waiting for their recursive call to finish
check.question: The call stack holds…

screens.heading: The call stack
screens.keyPoint: Waiting calls pile onto the call stack.

screens.body: Anything recursion can do, a loop can do. So when is recursion worth it? When the problem is naturally nested: folder trees, family trees, JSON, maze paths. If the data branches, recursion reads beautifully. If it's just counting, use a loop.
screens.heading: Recursion vs loops

screens.body: Naive fibonacci calls itself twice per level — fib(50) would make over a trillion calls. The two rules can't save you from a branching explosion. Lesson: recursion is elegant, but always ask how many calls you're really making.

options: Calls double every level — trillions of calls
check.question: Naive fib(50) is slow because…

screens.heading: The danger: exponential blowup
screens.keyPoint: Count your calls, not just your rules.
